facts.name: Smooth Blue Aster
facts.notes: A Michigan native aster with smooth, blue-green leaves and clouds of lavender-blue daisies from late summer into October, feeding native bees, butterflies and moths late in the year. Shorter than New England aster and happy in dry, sunny spots. Deer like to eat it.

sources.title: MSU Native Plants: Smooth blue aster
sources.note: Michigan native perennial in MSU's native plant trials; late bloomer (mid-August into early October) that draws pollinators and natural enemies.

sources.title: Wild Cherry Farm (Michigan native nursery): Smooth Aster
sources.note: Sold as a native plant by a Michigan nursery; a late bloomer native bees love.

sources.title: MSU Native Plants: Smooth blue aster fact sheet (PDF)
sources.note: Bloom period mid-August through early October; available as seed, plugs and potted plants from Michigan native plant nurseries.

sources.title: Roundstone Native Seed: Smooth Aster
sources.note: 2 to 3 ft tall; dry to medium, well-drained soil in full sun, tolerates damper sites in part shade.

sources.title: USDA NRCS Plant Guide: Smooth Blue Aster
sources.note: Palatable to white-tailed deer. Popular in wildflower, native and butterfly gardens.

companions.why: Pair with fall aster, bugbane, eupatorium, goldenrod, sedum or toad lily; near bleeding heart; with variegated hosta and grasses.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Japanese Anemone article

companions.why: Pair with dark-leaved Heuchera; combine with aster, tall sedums like 'Autumn Joy', yarrow, rudbeckias and purple coneflower.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Little Bluestem article

companions.why: Combines well with ornamental grasses, anise hyssop, beebalm, daylilies, fall asters, liatris, purple coneflower and rudbeckias.
